title.narrative: Addressing children who missed routine Measles immunization in the southern and southeastern areas of Ethiopia

description.narrative: Immunization is among the most successful and cost-effective health interventions ever devised. Between 2010 and 2018, globally 23 million deaths were averted with the measles vaccine alone. In Ethiopia, routine immunization coverage has been increasing steadily over the years. However, it has not been growing at the rate necessary to reach national, regional, and global targets, especially in the last three years due to conflicts, and natural and human-made disasters.According to the 2023 WUENIC report 10 countries account for 59% of "zero dose children including Ethiopia. Among the leading 10 countries for DTP zero-dose children, Ethiopia has placed second and third with 1.1m and 917k Penta zero-dose children in 2022 and 2023 respectively. and Ethiopia is also the third- and fourth-largest contributor to measles zero doses with 1.7 million and 1.6 million ZD children in 2022 and 2023 respectively. The ongoing conflict in the country as well as the draught in the southern and southeastern parts of the regions in Somali, Oromia, and Sothern nations has resulted in displacement of the people, immunization service interruption left so many children unvaccinated for Measles created fertile ground for VPD outbreaks.Six different forecast sources are converging on a consensus that the 2024 October to December rainy season will likely experience below-average rainfall, Drought conditions in Somali, Oromia, and Southeastern nations might be expanded in the areas where such episodes might previously not have been noticed. These droughts-affected regions are major contributors to the low national EPI performance in the country, the displacement due to draught has also caused significant immunization service interruption because of vaccine stock out, and the high number of health workers turnover. Failure to address children who have missed their immunization schedule in these regions will contribute to the ongoing active Measles outbreak. With this view, WCO for Ethiopia plans to support 38 prioritized woredas in the Somali, Oromia, and South Ethiopia regions through financial support from CERF. The project Objectives include improving measles vaccination coverage in the selected 38 Woredas in the southern and southeastern areas of Ethiopia (South Ethiopia, Somali and Oromia) by 10% from administrative baseline coverage by the end of 2025, Enabling health facilities to provide measles- vaccines through system strengthening in the selected 38 woredas and Improve the measles outbreak response capacity of the health system through training, sensitization, monitoring, and supportive supervision which will contribute to Measles elimination through strengthening primary health care. The project implementation and design will be guided by the above goals and consistent with the Immunization Global Agenda 2030, Afro Measles Elimination Strategy, and SDG3 goals. The project will address the above objective through Capacity building, enhanced Measles catch-up vaccination integrated with other essential health services, in draught-affected woredas in collaboration with MOH, Regional health bureaus, and other implementing partners in the areas. WHO and UNICEF will implement them in a complementary manner, UNICEF will handle vaccine procurement and distribution, demand creation, and communication activities whereas WHO will handle the micro-planning, training, monitoring, and overall coordination. Technical Assistance will be deployed to coordinate overall project implementation.The project will benefit 444,557 under-five-age children in the prioritized 38 drought-affected woredas of the Somali, Oromia, and South Ethiopia regions. The project willIncrease the routine measles vaccination coverage by 10% from the selected 38 woredas baseline by vaccinating 444,557 of the estimated children aged below five years.Capacitated and improved HFs to provide quality immunization services.The knowledge and skills of healthcare workers will be improved
